title: Bridging Quantum Computing Paradigms toward Semiconductor Yield: A Controlled CV-versus-DV Comparison on Wafer-Map Defect Classification
authors: Yeonhong Kim, Jonghyeok Im, Monu Nath Baitha, Kyoungsik Kim
abstract: Realizing quantum neural networks (QNNs) in industry requires knowing which quantum computing paradigm suits which task. Motivated by AI accelerators and high-bandwidth memory, where die stacking makes wafer-level defect screening central to yield, we study WM-811K wafer-map defect classification (eight classes), comparing the dominant paradigms, continuous-variable (CV) and discrete-variable (DV), under controlled conditions. To isolate the quantum circuit as the sole variable, a shared convolutional backbone (~4.3M parameters) feeds interchangeable heads (classical dense, CV-QNN, or DV-QNN) as the only structural difference; each quantum head is scaled over three sizes (3, 4, 8 qumodes/qubits). The CV head consistently outperforms the DV head: at four qumodes/qubits it reaches 79.7 +/- 1.8% accuracy versus 61.6 +/- 1.4%, a non-overlapping 18-point gap. The advantage is sharpest on the spatially localized Edge-Loc class, easily confused with Scratch, which CV recovers with recall 0.66 +/- 0.06 while DV fails at every size (<=0.05), showing the structured CV layer better captures fine spatial distinctions between defect types. Training curves show the DV limitation is a representational-capacity ceiling, not an optimization failure; at the Fock cutoff used here (d = 2) the CV advantage reflects two intrinsic properties, a structured, neural-network-analogue layer and continuous phase-space encoding, not Hilbert-space dimensionality. On IBM hardware, DV accuracy holds at shallow depth, degrading only at the deepest circuit. Both quantum heads remain below the classical baseline (85.0%), but the controlled setting isolates where a structured head already helps and, as noise and scale improve, which paradigm can deliver practical advantage.
summary: This work compares CV-QNNs against DV-QNNs for classifying semiconductor wafer defects using a controlled hybrid architecture. The results strongly indicate that CV approaches offer superior performance, especially when distinguishing subtle spatial defect patterns. This guides the choice of quantum paradigm for industrial AI acceleration.
main_problem: The study compares Continuous-Variable (CV) versus Discrete-Variable (DV) quantum neural network paradigms to determine which is best suited for high-stakes wafer-map defect classification in semiconductor manufacturing.
main_result: The CV head consistently outperforms the DV head, showing a significant advantage on spatially localized defects like Edge-Loc. This suggests structured continuous encoding is superior for this task.
method: A controlled evaluation protocol was used where only the quantum classification head (CV-QNN or DV-QNN) was varied while keeping the feature extraction CNN backbone identical.
model_or_system: The system involves classifying eight defect classes from a wafer map dataset (WM-811K). The models are hybrid, combining classical CNN features with quantum circuits operating on either continuous variables (CV) or discrete qubits (DV).
key_observables: Classification accuracy and recall, particularly for the spatially structured 'Edge-Loc' class.
important_parameters: Number of qumodes/qubits tested (3, 4, 8); input noise level ($\sigma$); circuit depth; feature vector dimension (512).
main_assumptions: The CV advantage is attributed to structured design and continuous phase-space encoding, not necessarily genuine non-Gaussianity at the tested cutoff ($d=2$).
figures_summary: Figures show performance comparisons across different defect classes, noise robustness sweeps (CV vs DV), and depth-resolved hardware accuracy degradation.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem context in semiconductor yield, details the controlled comparison setup (shared CNN backbone + interchangeable quantum heads), presents quantitative results showing CV superiority, diagnoses the physical limitations of DV circuits, and discusses implications for future quantum hardware design.
why_interesting: While focused on ML application, the rigorous comparison between continuous vs. discrete encoding methods provides insights into the fundamental representational power limits of different quantum information processing models.
